speakers: Cullen Roche (Pragmatic Capitalism, author and macro/behavioral investor)
summary:
Interview (Oct 2022) with Cullen Roche on his book Pragmatic Capitalism: macro as the river that stock pickers swim in, investing vs reallocating savings, time-horizon (All Duration) asset allocation with bond ladders, home bias and international diversification, why bonds are better value after the 2022 sell-off, banks as money creators, yield curve control and the Fed's financial-stability role.
Approach is education-oriented, low-frequency and behavioral; few testable signals.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the typical passive investor these days is really a macro investing approach
claims.claim: Passive indexing is effectively a macro approach (buy the whole market rather than pick needles) which has risen because information moves faster and the world economy is interconnected.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the world has become this very small place, in large part because of technology and just innovations that have made intercontinental trade and international trade just a
claims.claim: Because companies and banks are globally interconnected, macro and government policy matter more than in Buffett's era, e.g. trouble at a European bank can force the Fed to act through payment-system links.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: it’s equally important to understand the dynamics of the river
claims.claim: Stock picking is like finding the best swimmer, but the macro 'river' determines how fast everyone swims, so top-down macro understanding should come before security selection.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: income statements reflect the rivers and balance sheets are reflected by the lakes
claims.claim: Income statements are flows and balance sheets are stocks; policy such as QE operates as flows that accumulate in balance sheets, so understanding balance-sheet flows tells how policy will impact asset values.
claims.indicator: balance sheet flows from Fed operations

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: you could have a really sound understanding of the flow effects of something like quantitative easing.
claims.claim: Economic mechanics are predictable but investor responses (e.g. buying junk bonds after QE, meme stocks and crypto in 2020-21) are emotional and irrational, so one must also model the response mechanism.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: you’ve gotta be able to think, a few moves ahead to interpret well how is all this stuff gonna work
claims.claim: Investing requires second-level thinking like chess: even against a weak opponent, misjudging their responses to policy leads to trouble.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: in macro econ, the word investing means to spend for future production
claims.claim: In macroeconomics investment means spending for future production (e.g. a firm builds a factory), whereas buying stocks and bonds in secondary markets is technically reallocating savings with little impact on the firm.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: over the course of a 10 year period, 90% of corporations will fail
claims.claim: Real economic investment (starting firms) is high risk with about 90% failure over ten years, so retail savers should treat their portfolio as prudent reallocation of savings across cash, bonds and stocks, not a get-rich-quick bet.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: we don’t really talk that much about generating the best risk adjusted return across time
claims.claim: Asset allocation should be built around the timing of liabilities (monthly bills, car in 2 years, house in 5, retirement in 30) rather than optimizing return per unit of risk in a mean-variance framework.
claims.testable: partly: liability-matched portfolios can be simulated

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the beauty of a bond ladder is that if you have a hundred thousand dollars
claims.claim: A bond ladder (e.g. 10% of the allocation spread over one to ten year maturities and rolled annually) gives a near-certain short bucket for cash needs without regard to interest-rate forecasts.
claims.testable: yes: ladder returns vs duration-matched benchmark

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the stock market is an 18 year type of bond like instrument inside of my model
claims.claim: In the All Duration Investing model every asset gets a calculated duration (stocks about 18 years, also gold, commodities, REITs) to map assets to time horizons; the duration estimates involve guesswork.
claims.testable: partly: estimation method is not specified

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: you have to make the worst behavioral mistake you can, which is being a forced seller of stocks into a downturn because you just need the liquidity
claims.claim: Investors overweight stocks without short-term liquidity become forced sellers in a bear market (2022, S&P down 25%), the worst behavioral mistake, so hold cash and intermediate bonds for near-term needs.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the biggest biases I think in investing is being too short term and being too long term
claims.claim: Both day traders (short-term bias) and stocks-for-the-long-run believers (long-term bias) mis-match horizons; a 10-year bond cannot be turned into a 1-year bond.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: real estate historically is only generated about a one, maybe 2% real return
claims.claim: A home bought by a typical owner earns only about 1-2% real return after tax, maintenance and inflation, because owners do not count upkeep and taxes; outcomes depend on entry timing (2006 vs 2012).
claims.testable: yes: compare long-run real house price series with costs

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: you should assume that the aggregate stock market after inflation is probably only gonna do like four to 5%
claims.claim: Buffett suggests expecting only about 4-5% real stock market returns after inflation, taxes and fees, about half the 10% commonly cited, so controllable factors (fees, taxes, behavior) and human capital matter more.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the more active you are though, the less control you have because you’re incurring higher taxes and fees along the way
claims.claim: More active trading means higher taxes and fees and less control over outcomes, so day trading is a poor use of human capital compared with building valuable skills.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: if you only invested in the home bias. You missed out on all of these other economic booms internationally
claims.claim: Home bias is costly over long periods: a London investor in 1800 missed the rise of the US; Japanese investors in 1990 who held only Japanese stocks suffered while international portfolios did vastly better.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: reserve currencies come and they go the world’s superpowers. They ebb and they flow
claims.claim: Reserve currencies and superpowers rise and fall, so holding only S&P 500 stocks is a bet on continued US dominance; international revenues of US firms give partial diversification that might shrink with deglobalization.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: international stocks, for instance, they kick the pants off of US stocks in the two thousands
claims.claim: US and international equities alternate in long 15-20 year cycles (international outperformed in the 2000s, US since), and the cycle may be turning in 2022.
claims.indicator: US vs international equity relative performance

claims.speaker: Stig Brodersen
claims.quote: if you bought a global index, Japan would be 45%. And today it’s less than 5%
claims.claim: Japan's weight in global equity indices fell from about 45% in 1989 to under 5%, a warning on cap-weighted concentration in the winning country; international equities now cost only a few basis points more.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: over the course of a five or six or seven year period, when you let that bond mature, it will mature at par
claims.claim: In 2022 a 5-year bond down 15% will still mature at par and pay its coupon if held, so mark-to-market losses matter only for investors who must sell before maturity.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: when interest rates are at zero, your interest rate risk is just, it is completely different than when interest rates are starting at four
claims.claim: Interest-rate risk is far higher from zero rates because coupon income cannot cushion price losses: a 5-duration bond with a 5% coupon loses all its coupon from a 1% rate rise, while a 10% coupon would need two years of principal loss to offset.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: when interest rates rise, the prices fall, their future returns become better
claims.claim: Like stocks, bonds that fall in price have higher future returns; the 1970s were not terrible for bonds held as income because higher yields were rolled into.
claims.indicator: bond yield as predictor of forward return

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: a much far superior value today than they were because interest rates have risen
claims.claim: In Oct 2022 with yields of 5-6% bonds are much better value than in the zero-rate period, and the likelihood of rates continuing to rise at this pace is lower.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: I really do not think people should think of bonds as being a real return protecting type of instrument
claims.claim: Bonds (and T-bills at 4%) provide nominal principal stability over defined horizons, not real returns, which is why TIPS are not a favored tool; use maturities within about 5 years to avoid large interest-rate risk.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: you have to build a portfolio where you do end up kind of hating a portion of your portfolio
claims.claim: Diversification requires holding uncorrelated assets some of which will lag; value lagged growth for a decade then 'smoked' it in 2021-22, and a blended portfolio avoids timing the market.
claims.indicator: value vs growth, cash, bonds, gold, commodities

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the investor that owns gold or commodities or even bonds in this environment, well what they’ve done is they’ve buffered the negative 25% return in the stock market
claims.claim: In 2022 stocks fell 25% while bonds fell 11%, gold 10% and commodities rose, so a diversified mix buffered stock losses and cut behavioral stress.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: when all those things are correlated one to one, they’re correlated negatively in a really bad way
claims.claim: In short-term stress, assets that are all highly correlated hurt together, whereas cash (down 7-8% real but 0% nominal in 2022) became the best part of the portfolio.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: loans create deposits and deposits for all practical purposes or money
claims.claim: Banks create most money (loans create deposits); central bank reserves lent to banks do not drive loan creation, which depends on loan demand and credit-worthy borrowers.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: when the government runs huge deficits, what they’re really doing is they’re giving a bond generally to a rich person
claims.claim: Large deficits financed by bonds to rich savers and spent to people with higher marginal propensity to spend amount to money printing in the traditional sense, whereas central bank reserve creation does not reach the private sector.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: they’re controlling the quantity of bonds, they’re not controlling the price of bonds
claims.claim: Quantitative easing is less effective than assumed because the central bank sets the quantity of long bonds, not the price, whereas at the short end it sets the overnight price as a monopolist; yield curve control would set long yields explicitly.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: the 10 year yield lower than the two year today, the marketplace is basically saying we are not as worried about inflation as the Federal Reserve is
claims.claim: An inverted yield curve (10-year below 2-year) signals that the market expects lower long-term inflation than the Fed and that policy is too tight, which is why the curve predicts recessions.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: in terms of their third mandate, that really is it’s to sustain financial stability
claims.claim: The Fed's third mandate is financial stability via payment-system clearing; before the Fed, private clearing houses broke down in panics (1907), and central banks are good at resolving them as in 2008.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: I think quantitative easing is a bad policy
claims.claim: Roche opposes QE and discretionary 'fingers in the air' rate setting, preferring systematic rules.

claims.speaker: Cullen Roche
claims.quote: trying to control for investor behavior is actually probably one of the most important things we can try to do
claims.claim: Discipline-based investing, controlling behavior, is one of the most important determinants of investor outcomes.
